summary: Find the one element that appears once in a sorted array where all others appear twice, in O(log n).
mainInsight: Before the single element, pairs start at even indices (nums[2k] == nums[2k + 1]); after it, the pairing shifts to odd indices. Binary search on even indices: if nums[mid] equals its partner, the single element is to the right, otherwise it is at mid or to the left.

approaches.name: Binary search on pair parity
approaches.summary: Compare nums[mid] with the partner at mid ^ 1.

personalSolution.approach: Binary search comparing nums[mid] with both neighbours and branching on the parity of mid
personalSolution.notes: Optimal complexity, but the boundary special cases make it error-prone; aligning mid to the first slot of a pair needs only one comparison.

commonMistakes: Not forcing mid to be even
Using nums[mid + 1] without a bounds check

promptVariants: Why force mid to be even and compare nums[mid] with nums[mid + 1]?
What does a match imply about where the single element is?
cards.answer: If mid is odd, step back to the even index mid - 1, so mid is always the first slot of a pair. If nums[mid] == nums[mid + 1] the pairs are still aligned up to mid + 1, so the single element lies to the right (lo = mid + 2); otherwise the alignment has already shifted, so the single element is at mid or to its left (hi = mid). (Equivalently compare nums[mid] with nums[mid ^ 1].)
keyPoints: Force mid to the first slot of a pair
Match => single is to the right
Mismatch => single at mid or left
cards.explanation: XOR of all elements is the O(n) alternative.

promptVariants: Your solution handles the boundaries with several special cases. How does the pair-aligned version avoid them?
Which part of your condition could be removed by forcing mid onto an even index?
cards.answer: Your code checks neighbours on both sides, so it needs separate cases for n == 1, mid == 0 and mid == n - 1 to avoid reading outside the array and an explicit chained test for 'neither neighbour equals nums[mid]'. Forcing mid onto the first slot of a pair and comparing only with nums[mid + 1] needs a single comparison with no boundary cases, because the array length is odd and the search range always keeps an odd number of elements.
keyPoints: Compare only with the partner mid + 1
Odd length and even mid keep indices in range
cards.explanation: Choosing an invariant (pair alignment) can replace several case checks.
Halving the search range each step.
